name: dvanalyzer
desc: Quality control tool for examining tape-to-file DV streams
why: Examines raw DV tape-to-file streams for errors, a rare look at how digital video bits are laid down on tape.

brief.what_it_is: DV Analyzer is a technical quality control and reporting tool that examines DV streams, the raw DV data produced when a DV tape (miniDV, DVCam, DVCPro) is transferred to a file. It reports errors introduced in the tape-to-file transfer, such as video error concealment information, invalid audio samples, timecode inconsistency, inconsistent use of arbitrary bits in video DIF blocks, and DIF structural problems. It also reports patterns in the DV stream, such as changes in DV time code, changes in recording date and time markers, and first and last frame markers within individual recordings. The input is a DV file and the output is a per-frame analysis and report.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says the tape-to-file reformatting of DV is a point where permanent errors are of particularly high risk, and that most capture tools only report errors when they are significant, such as a lost frame, while other documented errors go unreviewed. The tool is meant to enable automated quality control and to verify the accuracy and integrity of the reformatting on a frame-by-frame basis. It was initially funded, designed and led by AVPreserve and is developed by MediaArea.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage describes the tool as analyzing and reporting audio, video, subcode, and structural errors within a DV file, and as interpreting the temporal metadata carried in every DV frame (time code, recording date and time, recording markers). It has views and documents that present this information, and the homepage links to a case study with sample DV files and explanations of detected errors, including Final Cut Pro XML temporal metadata, video error concealment, audio errors, DIF incoherency, and STTS fluctuation. I did not find a description of the internal implementation.
brief.install_notes: Binaries are provided for Windows, macOS, Debian, Ubuntu, Linux Mint, RedHat Enterprise Linux, CentOS, Fedora, openSUSE, ArchLinux, Flatpak, and other systems, per the homepage. The homepage lists version 1.4.2 and links to a ChangeLog and to very recent snapshots. The GitHub repository has separate CLI and GUI history files, which suggests both a command-line and a graphical interface exist, but I did not verify this from a README. I saw no hardware, account, or runtime requirements, and no first-run steps.
brief.standout: Few tools look at the raw DV bitstream this closely; most capture tools only flag gross failures like dropped frames. It is aimed at digital preservation QC and reads the per-frame temporal metadata that DV carries. It is produced by MediaArea with AVPreserve's original funding and is GPL-licensed.
brief.status: Probably maintained, but I cannot confirm dates. The homepage shows version 1.4.2 as the current download. The GitHub repository (MediaArea/DVAnalyzer) shows 82 commits, 13 stars, 8 forks, and a GPL-3.0 license. I could not see a last-release or last-commit date in the fetched pages, so the status is unknown.
brief.caveats: I could not read a project README. The GitHub page returned the GPL-3.0 license text in place of a README, and the homepage has no usage examples or command syntax, so I could not describe how to run it. Platform support beyond the listed systems is unknown. The homepage asks visitors to donate to support further development. The code is GPLv3+.
quotes: DV Analyzer is a technical quality control and reporting tool that examines DV streams in order to report errors in the tape-to-file transfer process
Most capture tools for DV only report errors if they are significant, such as a lost frame, whereas other documented errors are not reviewed.
It is Open-Source software which means that end users and developers have freedom to study, to improve and to redistribute the program (GPLv3+ for the code developed by us).

judge.reason: It exposes hidden structure and transfer errors in DV tape streams frame by frame, making a niche preservation workflow a genuinely interesting way to explore digital video.

entry.title: DV Analyzer
entry.tldr: Reads a DV video file frame by frame and reports the tape-transfer errors most capture tools never mention, from concealed video blocks to timecode jumps.
entry.deeper_look:
DV Analyzer examines the raw DV stream you get when a miniDV, DVCam or DVCPro tape is copied to a file. It reports problems introduced in that transfer: video error concealment, invalid audio samples, timecode inconsistency, odd use of arbitrary bits in video DIF blocks, and structural DIF problems. It also reads patterns in the stream, such as changes in timecode, recording date and time markers, and the first and last frame of each recording.

The reason it exists is stated on the homepage: tape-to-file reformatting is a point where permanent errors are at particularly high risk, and "Most capture tools for DV only report errors if they are significant, such as a lost frame, whereas other documented errors are not reviewed." The tool aims to make automated quality control possible, checking the integrity of a transfer frame by frame. It was initially funded, designed and led by AVPreserve and is developed by MediaArea.

The idea underneath is that a DV frame carries more than picture and sound. Every frame holds its own temporal metadata, so a file is a long record of how the tape was recorded and how it was read back. That makes it a way into digital video preservation and into how a consumer tape format lays its data out in small blocks. The homepage links a case study with sample DV files covering concealment, audio errors, DIF incoherency and STTS fluctuation.
entry.install:
brew install dvanalyzer

It needs a DV file to analyze. Tape hardware is only needed if you want to capture your own.

try_this.what_happens: Prints the command-line options, which is the safest place to start since no usage examples were found in the project's pages.

entry.whats_unique: Few tools look at the raw DV bitstream this closely. It is built for preservation QC and surfaces per-frame errors and temporal metadata that capture software usually ignores.
entry.caveats: No README or usage examples were found, so the command syntax is unconfirmed, and the status and last release date are unknown, though the homepage lists version 1.4.2.
